prompt: Which of these is an assertion title?
hint: It has a verb and a claim.

choices.text: Cancellations by region
choices.why: A topic: it names what the slide is about.

choices.text: Results of the first-delivery study
choices.why: Still a topic, only longer.

choices.text: Late first deliveries and cancellations
choices.why: Two nouns joined by "and" is a topic; there is no verb.

choices.text: The gap holds in both regions
choices.why: A complete sentence stating what the chart shows.

prompt: With a topic title, what does the reader do first, by the lesson?
hint: Then they listen to find out whether it matches.

choices.text: Reads the chart with no idea what to look for, and forms a conclusion
choices.why: Then they compare it with yours, instead of listening.

choices.text: Skips the slide
choices.why: They still look; they just look without a target.

choices.text: Asks a question
choices.why: Not the lesson's description.

choices.text: Checks the claim in the chart
choices.why: That is what an assertion title makes possible; a topic gives no claim to check.

prompt: What did Michael Alley's studies with engineering students find, as the lesson reports them?

choices.text: Bullet points improve recall by a fixed percentage in every kind of setting
choices.why: The finding favoured assertion–evidence slides, and the lesson warns against a precise number outside the classroom.

choices.text: No difference between slide styles
choices.why: There was one.

choices.text: Better understanding with assertion–evidence slides
choices.why: Measured on technical material in a classroom; reasonable to expect in a meeting.

choices.text: Audiences prefer shorter titles
choices.why: The sentence titles were the longer ones.

prompt: Which are rules for a good assertion title? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A complete sentence with a verb
choices.why: Otherwise it is a topic.

choices.text: Says what the chart shows, no more
choices.why: Two bars cannot support a claimed trend.

choices.text: Fits in two lines
choices.why: Past that it is a paragraph.

choices.text: Never contains a number
choices.why: When the number is the point, it belongs in the title.

prompt: What is a ghost deck?

choices.text: A deck that is prepared but nobody ends up presenting
choices.why: It is presented, after it is filled.

choices.text: Titles only, written before any chart
choices.why: Circulated and argued over while changes cost seconds.

choices.text: An appendix, kept after the last slide for questions
choices.why: The appendix holds evidence; the ghost deck holds the story.

choices.text: A template with the company's colours and fonts
choices.why: A template is design; a ghost deck is content.

prompt: Why write the titles before making charts?

choices.text: Because charts take longer to load in the slide tool
choices.why: Not about software.

choices.text: So the story decides which charts are made
choices.why: A chart no title asks for is never made.

choices.text: Titles are more important than charts
choices.why: They do different jobs; the order is about which drives which.

choices.text: To leave the charts to a designer
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson hands them off.

prompt: A colleague reads only your titles and cannot tell the story back. Which are the likely causes, by the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A topic title slipped through
choices.why: It names without saying.

choices.text: A slide carries two messages
choices.why: One title cannot say both.

choices.text: A step between two titles that you know and they do not
choices.why: Obvious to you, missing for them.

choices.text: The charts are too small
choices.why: The test reads titles only; charts are not involved.

prompt: How many titles are in Faro's ghost deck?
hint: Answer, context, conflict, three supports, request.

prompt: Match each message to the chart that shows its comparison.

pairs.left: Late first boxes more than double cancellations
The gap holds in both regions
First deliveries are a sliver of the total
The rate has not improved all year

prompt: Why is the four-line monthly chart wrong under Marina's title?

choices.text: The data in it is wrong
choices.why: The chart is correct.

choices.text: Lines cannot show rates
choices.why: They can; this one answers another question.

choices.text: Six months is too short a period to show any trend at all
choices.why: Not the problem.

choices.text: It answers another comparison than the title's
choices.why: It shows stability over time; the title compares two groups.

prompt: Where should the monthly lines go?
hint: They answer whether the gap is stable.

choices.text: In the appendix, for whoever asks if the gap was a one-month accident
choices.why: A good answer to a different question.

choices.text: In the first slide
choices.why: The first slide is the answer.

choices.text: Nowhere
choices.why: They are useful; just not under this title.

choices.text: Beside the two bars on the same slide
choices.why: Two charts, two messages.

prompt: A chart for a message has as few ___ as the comparison needs.
What is the most reliable emphasis technique in the lesson?

choices.text: Bold every number
choices.why: Everything bold means nothing bold.

choices.text: A different colour per bar
choices.why: That makes every bar equally loud.

choices.text: Grey first, then one colour
choices.why: The eye goes to the colour before the title is finished.

choices.text: A 3D effect on the important bar
choices.why: Decoration that competes with the data.

prompt: Why label bars directly instead of using a legend?
hint: Where does the eye have to go?

choices.text: A legend makes the reader look away and back
choices.why: Direct labels keep the eye on the data and cannot be misread.

choices.text: Legends are not allowed by the design guidelines of most companies
choices.why: No such rule is given.

choices.text: Legends cost colours
choices.why: Not the reason.

choices.text: Labels make bars wider
choices.why: They do not.

prompt: An annotation on the chart repeats the title. What does the lesson say about that?
hint: How long does each get looked at?

choices.text: Remove it, because repetition wastes ink
choices.why: Here the repetition earns its place.

choices.text: Keep it only for the board
choices.why: It helps every room.

choices.text: Move it to the speaker notes
choices.why: The room never sees speaker notes.

choices.text: Fine: the title is read once, the chart looked at for a minute
choices.why: The point belongs in both places.

prompt: Why must colour never be the only thing that tells two bars apart?

choices.text: Projectors wash colours out in a bright meeting room
choices.why: True sometimes, and not the reason given.

choices.text: Some readers cannot tell them apart
choices.why: A label or a pattern keeps the chart readable for them.

choices.text: Colour is reserved for the logo
choices.why: No.

choices.text: It costs more to print a colour handout for everyone
choices.why: Not the argument.

prompt: Which is a sign that a slide carries two messages?

choices.text: It has one chart and an assertion title of a single line
choices.why: That is the healthy case.

choices.text: You say "also" while presenting it
choices.why: "This shows the gap… and also…" is two messages.

choices.text: It has a number in the title
choices.why: Numbers are welcome in titles.

choices.text: It is in the appendix
choices.why: Location says nothing about message count.

prompt: One chart genuinely holds two steps of the argument. What does the lesson suggest?

choices.text: Two titles on one slide
choices.why: That is two messages at once.

choices.text: Remove one of the steps
choices.why: Both belong to the argument.

choices.text: Build it up: first part, then the same slide with the second added
choices.why: Each step has one message, and the comparison stays on one set of axes.

choices.text: Put the chart in the appendix
choices.why: It is evidence the story needs.

prompt: You split a slide carrying two messages into two slides. What happens to the length of the talk, by the lesson?

choices.text: Shorter: each one is understood at once
choices.why: A slide that needs explaining costs more minutes than two that do not.

choices.text: Longer, because every extra slide adds a transition and an introduction
choices.why: The transition is cheap; explaining a crowded slide is not.

choices.text: The same, since the content does not change
choices.why: The content is the same and the time to understand it is not.

choices.text: It depends on how many bullet points each slide has
choices.why: Bullets are not the measure.

prompt: This slide has five problems. Put each label on the one it names.
hint: The bars at the top stand for words.

labels.text: a legend far from its data
a title too long for one message
